title: Poe Alternatives: Best Options Compared (2026 Guide)
summary: Poe alternatives have different pricing models than Poe's credits. Identify which one will cost less based on how much you use AI models.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces


Expect more setup than Poe asks for, not less.


Activepieces suits only readers who used Poe bots for repeatable work such as summarizing, drafting or routing, rather than for conversation, and the free plan's 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows are enough to find out which kind you are.


### What it replaces and what it does not


You build a flow in Activepieces, an open-source workflow automation platform with an MIT-licensed core and 747 integrations: a trigger starts it, steps run in order, and an AI step calls a model with a prompt you write, so cross-platform automation becomes practical.


It can also pause for a human approval before anything goes out. That covers the bots people built in Poe to process the same kind of input again and again.


It does not replace the chat window. There's no place to ask a question, compare two models side by side, or follow up on an answer. If that's why you pay for Poe, keep Poe or pick a chat-first tool.


### Price and hosting


Activepieces holds the trigger, the AI step, shared tables, MCP tools and the approval gate in one product, with RBAC, SSO, SCIM, audit logs, environments and git sync covering all of it, on cloud or self-hosted.


Integration the same span together from point tools and a misfiring bot sends you through six vendors and six bills to work out what happened; MoneyGram and Moneypenny run Activepieces in production.


The catch is upkeep: updates, backups and uptime become your job. The hosted cloud version removes that work in exchange for a plan fee, which suits anyone whose time costs more than a server.


### Which Poe tasks to move first


Start with the bot whose output you copy somewhere else by hand. That copying's the step a flow removes. The sequence below is the shape of nearly every replacement, so a reader can use it as a checklist for the first one:


1. Pick the trigger: a new form entry, an incoming email, or a schedule.
2. Add the AI step and paste in the prompt your Poe bot used, mapping the incoming data into it.
3. Add an approval step so a person reviews the output before it goes anywhere.
4. Connect the output app, such as your document tool, spreadsheet or email.
5. Turn the flow on, then open the run log and confirm each step did what you expected.


Run the first few cases with the approval step in place. The run log shows where a prompt misfired, which a chat window never made visible.


Once the output holds up, you can decide whether the approval step stays for every run or only for the risky ones.


Activepieces is the better choice for teams and individuals who used Poe bots for repeatable work such as summarizing, drafting or routing, and who need that work to run under real governance.


That means RBAC, SSO, SCIM, audit logs, log and event streaming, and environments with git sync, all in one product, self-hosted or on cloud, with no cut-down version either way.


It asks for more setup than Poe does, and readers who mainly want conversation with a model will not gain from it, but for repeatable, controlled automation it covers in one platform what other tools sell in pieces.
